771.quote_or_event: “The battle-drum beats in the sky of the mind; aim is taken, and the wound is inflicted. The spiritual warriors enter the field of battle; now is the time to fight!”
771.explanation: Bhagat Kabir's salok uses the language of the battlefield, with drums, aim and the hero entering the field, to call the seeker to the inner fight.
771.tie_back: The Kural gives a warrior's defiant battlefield cry to the enemy; Kabir's salok has the same martial ring of a hero announcing that the hour of battle has come.
771.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1105, Raag Maaroo, Salok Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
771._accuracy_note: Shares the battle-cry tone only; Kabir's battle is spiritual, and nothing here matches the Kural's warning to the enemy or its hero-stones.

772.quote_or_event: “See the brotherhood of all mankind as the highest order of Yogis; conquer your own mind, and conquer the world.”
772.explanation: In Japji Sahib Guru Nanak names the mind as the real adversary worth defeating; whoever masters it has won everything.
772.tie_back: The Kural says it is nobler to aim at an elephant and miss than to kill a hare; Guru Nanak points the seeker toward the hardest of all enemies, one's own mind, rather than easy victories.
772.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 6, Japji Sahib, Pauri 28, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
772._accuracy_note: Matches the idea of choosing the worthiest adversary, but says nothing about honourable failure, which is the Kural's real point; a next-best match.

773.quote_or_event: During the siege of Anandpur (1704-05), Bhai Kanhaiya carried water to wounded soldiers of both armies without distinction. When Sikhs complained to Guru Gobind Singh that he was helping the enemy, Kanhaiya said he saw only the Guru's face in every man; the Guru approved and gave him ointment to treat the wounds as well.
773.explanation: Bhai Kanhaiya became the founder of the Sevapanthi order, and his service to wounded enemies is a central Sikh example of seva without enmity.
773.tie_back: The Kural calls help given to an enemy in his misfortune the sharp edge of valour; Bhai Kanhaiya, with the Guru's blessing, gave exactly that help on the battlefield.
773._accuracy_note: A near one-to-one match of mercy to the fallen foe within a war; the exact dialogue varies between tellings, but the core event is well attested in Sikh tradition.

774.quote_or_event: “Kabir! The world is afraid of death - that death fills my mind with bliss. It is only by death that perfect, supreme bliss is obtained.”
774.explanation: Kabir turns the common fear of death on its head; for one who has died to ego, death holds only joy.
774.tie_back: The Kural's hero smiles as he pulls a spear out of his own body; Kabir likewise meets what the world fears most with joy rather than dread.
774.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1365, Salok Bhagat Kabir (salok 22) (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
774._accuracy_note: Shares the joyful fearlessness, but Kabir means spiritual death of the ego and union with God, not delight in fighting on; a next-best match.

775.quote_or_event: Bhai Mati Das went with Guru Tegh Bahadur to Delhi in 1675 and was arrested with him. When he refused to give up his faith he was sawn in two from the head downwards; Sikh tradition adds that he went on reciting Japji to the end.
775.explanation: Bhai Mati Das is remembered daily in the Sikh Ardas among those who did not waver under the saw.
775.tie_back: The Kural says that for the truly brave even a blink before the enemy's spear counts as retreat; Bhai Mati Das is honoured precisely because he showed no sign of flinching under torture.
775.source: The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism, 'Mati Das, Bhai (d. 1675)' (paraphrase); the Japji detail follows devotional tradition
775._accuracy_note: A strong parallel for unflinching courage, but it is a martyr's steadfastness under execution, not a warrior in battle, and the recitation detail is traditional rather than documented.

776.quote_or_event: “You fill your belly, and sleep like an animal; you have wasted and lost this human life.”
776.explanation: Kabir rebukes a life given to eating and sleeping, saying it squanders the human birth meant for remembering God.
776.tie_back: The Kural's hero counts as wasted every day without an honourable wound; Kabir likewise counts as wasted a life spent in comfort rather than in its true purpose.
776.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1105, Raag Maaroo, Bhagat Kabir (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
776._accuracy_note: Only the idea that comfortable days are wasted days carries over; Kabir's measure is remembrance of God, not wounds, so this is a next-best match.

777.quote_or_event: “If you desire to play this game of love with Me, then step onto My Path with your head in hand. When you place your feet on this Path, give Me your head, and do not pay any attention to public opinion.”
777.explanation: Guru Nanak asks the seeker to come ready to give up life itself; Sikh tradition links this salok to the Khalsa's founding call for heads in 1699.
777.tie_back: The Kural says the warrior's anklet suits only those who do not cling to life; Guru Nanak says the path is open only to one who comes with his head on his palm.
777.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1412, Salok Vaaraan Thay Vadheek, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
777._accuracy_note: A strong match for not clinging to life, though Guru Nanak tells the seeker to ignore public opinion, while the Kural prizes world-encircling fame.

778.quote_or_event: “If my body were afflicted with pain, under the evil influence of unlucky stars; and if the blood-sucking kings were to hold power over me - even if this were my condition, I would still worship and adore You, and my longing to chant Your Praises would not decrease.”
778.explanation: Guru Nanak declares that no suffering and no oppressive ruler could lessen his eagerness to praise God.
778.tie_back: The Kural's warriors lose none of their fervour even when the king angrily holds them back; Guru Nanak's longing likewise does not diminish under hostile kings.
778.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 142, Raag Maajh (Vaar Maajh, salok), Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
778._accuracy_note: Strong on undiminished zeal under a ruler's power, but the kings here are tyrants, not the warriors' own lord restraining them, and the zeal is devotional, not martial.

779.quote_or_event: During the siege of Anandpur some forty Sikhs signed a disclaimer (bedava) renouncing Guru Gobind Singh and went home. Shamed by Mai Bhago, they returned and died fighting the pursuing Mughal force at Khidrana on 29 December 1705. According to tradition, the Guru tore up the disclaimer at the request of the dying Mahan Singh and blessed them as the Chali Mukte, the Forty Liberated Ones; Khidrana became Muktsar.
779.explanation: Their death in faithful battle wiped out their earlier failure, and they are remembered in the daily Ardas.
779.tie_back: The Kural asks who could blame those who die keeping their vow, even if the vow was not fulfilled; the Chali Mukte had broken faith, yet by dying for the Guru they were freed of all blame.
779.source: The Encyclopaedia of Sikhism, 'Chali Mukte' (paraphrase); the torn bedava follows Sikh tradition
779._accuracy_note: A close match for death in fidelity removing all reproach, especially under Pappaiah's reading; the number and names of the forty, and some details, vary between sources.

780.quote_or_event: “The death of brave heroes is blessed, if it is approved by God.”
780.explanation: In his Alahanian (dirges), Guru Nanak says death need not be called bad, and that the hero's death is worthy when it is accepted in God's court.
780.tie_back: The Kural says a death that brings tears to the eyes of the king who cared for the warrior is worth begging for; Guru Nanak likewise honours the hero's death, measuring its worth by the approval of the true Master.
780.source: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 579, Raag Vadhans, Alahanian, Guru Nanak (tr. Sant Singh Khalsa)
780._accuracy_note: A strong fit for a death made precious by the one who judges it, though the judge here is God rather than an earthly king, and there are no tears.
